name: Bianca Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for agreeing to this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say out loud and what you really think. To begin, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a flow-wrapper on the packing line at a biscuit factory, the big one by the canal. A flow-wrapper is the machine that seals biscuits into those plastic sleeves, so I'm feeding film reels, fixing misfeeds and watching the seal temperature. I've only been there ten months, so the old hands still beat me on clearing a jam, but I'm catching up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle when the line stops and you have to work out why. I've started asking an AI chatbot about the error codes on my break, and it's often faster than the manual. What wears me out is standing in one spot for eight hours, and the smell of sugar that never leaves your hair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold, and I'd still use it for the little stuff. I'd probably post a meme about all the people who swore their job was gone. At work nobody would care, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the plan I already have still works. I want to move from running the wrapper to fixing it, so I'm learning PLCs, the little computers that control the line. My partner Kofi tests software for a bank, and his job's safe in this picture too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my shifts and keep studying PLCs two evenings a week with an online course and the chatbot. I'd ask the engineering manager about the apprentice technician scheme next spring. I'd keep putting money aside, because I've already got about ten months saved from my warehouse years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit impatient, because I like change and this one's dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the ten months of savings come from, if you don't mind me asking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lived at my mum's for four years while I worked at a parcel warehouse, and I paid her a bit but banked the rest. I'm a bit obsessive about it. Having a cushion is what lets me take chances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still worries you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The packing line's on a temporary contract renewal with a supermarket, and rumours go round every year. If the supermarket walks, they cut a shift. That's not AI, that's just how food factories are.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, but I'd still use it for small things.
I'd post a **meme** about people who swore their jobs were finished.
think: My plan to move from running the wrapper to **fixing it** still works.
My partner's **bank testing** job stays safe in this picture too.
do: Study **PLCs** two evenings a week with an online course and a chatbot.
Ask the engineering manager about the **apprentice technician** scheme next spring.
feel: She feels **calm**, a little **impatient** because this version is dull.
S0.quote: Having a cushion is what lets me take chances.
fieldNote: Her savings come from **four years** living at her mother's, and she guards them.
The real local risk is a **supermarket contract**, not AI.
She already has a clear **technician** path and is working on it.

steps.text: Study PLC programming two evenings a week online
Keep running the flow-wrapper on her current shifts
Keep banking part of every pay on top of ten months saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance if workers get a say, and a disaster if they don't. I'd be in the union group pushing for training time on paid hours. And I'd tell people to start using the tools now, not fear them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried for my own job yet, because robots creep in slowly and I'm learning to fix them. The one I'm worried about is Kofi. Software testing is exactly the checking work the card is talking about, and his team has already lost two people who weren't replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push hard for the apprentice technician place this year, even if it means a pay cut at first. Help Kofi update his CV and look at roles where he sets up the testing tools instead of doing the tests. We'd hold off on buying a car and keep both savings pots topped up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but mostly on Kofi's behalf. My own path feels okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kofi if his team got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Kofi that my pay covers the rent for a year and he can take his time finding the right thing. I'd mean it too. He carried me when I left the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take a pay cut for the apprenticeship. Is that safe with Kofi's job at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a gamble, I know. But apprentice rates only last two years, and after that technicians earn more than I do now. With our savings, we could survive one of us dropping for a while, just not both.

say: I'd say AI is a **chance** if workers get a say and a disaster if not.
I'd push for **paid training time** and tell people to use the tools now.
think: My own job is fine for now because **robots** creep into packing slowly.
My partner's **software testing** job is exactly the checking work AI takes first.
do: Apply for the **apprentice technician** place this year, accepting lower pay at first.
Help her partner retarget his CV towards **setting up** test tools.
Delay buying a **car** and keep both savings pots topped up.
feel: She feels **anxious**, mostly for her **partner**, while her own path feels okay.
S1.quote: With our savings, we could survive one of us dropping for a while, just not both.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **household**, not herself: her partner is the exposed earner.
She'd take a **pay cut** for training, a bold move backed by savings.
She sees union action and **personal learning** as going together.

steps.text: Apply for the apprentice technician scheme despite lower starting pay
Push the union for training time on paid hours
Cover the rent alone if Kofi's testing team gets cut
Put off buying a car for at least a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs emergency rules, like a guaranteed income while people retrain, and I'd say it loudly. I'd march if there was a march. Online I'd share practical stuff, like which courses are still worth doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Kofi's job is gone by 2028, because AI does testing better and cheaper. Mine lasts until about 2031, and then a robot feeds film reels and clears jams. Even fixing robots might shrink later, so both our incomes are on a timer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the technician training straight away, not next spring, and pay for extra courses myself if the factory won't. Get Kofi into anything hands-on, maybe the electrician apprenticeship his uncle keeps offering, because hands-on buys three more years. Cut spending hard and save every spare penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It would keep me up. I'd have a plan, but two plans failing at once is scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the most comfortable with change of anyone I've spoken to. Why so worried here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because liking change doesn't help if the change is everyone at once. I'd be competing for a technician slot with half the line. Being quick only matters if you're quicker than everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday we booked for next summer, and the gym. We'd go down to one phone contract and cook every night. I'd sell my mum's old car that I barely drive.

say: I'd call for **emergency rules**, like a guaranteed income while people retrain.
I'd march, and share **practical advice** online about which courses are still worth doing.
think: My partner's **testing job** is likely gone by 2028 when AI arrives.
My hands-on job lasts until about **2031**, so both incomes are on a timer.
do: Start **technician training** immediately and pay for extra courses herself.
Steer her partner into a **hands-on** electrician apprenticeship for three more years.
Cancel the **summer holiday**, drop the gym and sell the old car.
feel: She feels **alarmed** and sleepless, because two plans could fail at once.
S2.quote: Liking change doesn't help if the change is everyone at once.
fieldNote: Even the most adaptive person feels **alarmed** when both household incomes are exposed.
She understands the **three-year gap** and steers her partner towards hands-on work.
Her insight: speed only helps if you're **quicker than others**.

steps.text: Start technician training now and pay for extra courses herself
March and campaign for income support during retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste the first three arguing. I'd push the union and the council to set up a robot technician course at the college now. I'd keep telling people to start using AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me. I'd be a qualified technician by 2029 and have a few years fixing robots before they get really good. Kofi's job hits in 2031, so he's got time to move into something hands-on or something that manages the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, then look at automation engineering at a bigger plant. Keep the savings growing and maybe put some into a small flat. Kofi would start an evening course in 2027 rather than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can live with. More like busy than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gita on the next wrapper, who's in her fifties and can't read English well. AI tools won't help her if they only speak in long paragraphs. I'd want the union to get training in plain language for people like her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently from the fast picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't sell the car or cancel holidays. I'd invest more instead of cutting, because there's time for it to pay off. Five years is a planning problem, two years is an emergency.

I'd push for a **robot technician** course at the local college right now.

steps.text: Finish the apprentice technician scheme by 2029
Put part of her savings into a small flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, and if it goes badly it's because someone chose not to plan. I'd keep pushing for the gains to be shared. At work I'd be the annoying one telling everyone to learn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is good for me. By 2039 I'd be 40, an engineer, maybe a supervisor in a plant that's mostly robots. Kofi would be okay too, because he's clever and has time to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the apprenticeship, then a part-time engineering degree in my thirties. Use AI to study, because it's patient and it's free at midnight. Kofi and I would probably get married and buy a house in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, about friends who won't move. But mostly excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good day at work look like in 2039 for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me with a tablet walking a line of robots, catching a fault before it stops anything, with no sugar in my hair. I wouldn't be standing at the wrapper all day. That sounds great to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for all that training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies who save the wages, and some from the government. I paid for my own PLC course, and I could, but most of the line couldn't.

I'd keep pushing for **shared gains** and nag colleagues to learn something new.
think: Ten years is **good** for me; by 2039 I could be an engineer.
My partner is **clever** and has time to switch fields too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Kofi and I would both be on a countdown at the same time. What would help is income support while you retrain, so people aren't choosing between a course and the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the one who's excited. Some of the older women on the line think I'm cheering for the robots. I'm not, I just want to be the one holding the tablet when the robots come.

headlineQuote: I just want to be the one holding the tablet when the robots come.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old** flow-wrapper operator at a biscuit factory, ten months in.
She has ten months of **savings** and is teaching herself PLCs with an AI chatbot.
Her partner tests software, so the **household** is exposed even when her job isn't.
She is calm if AI stalls, **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, and excited with a decade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her partner would both be on a **countdown** at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** during retraining, so people don't choose between a course and rent.
